title: Facet-Level Detective
summary: Two fictional people share a broad domain score almost exactly and behave quite differently. Students assign behavioural evidence before the facet scores are shown, build their own matched pair, then watch the "fixed" broad score reverse its ranking when the questionnaire samples facets differently.
learningObjectives: Explain why a broad domain score, being an average of narrower facets, cannot distinguish two people who reach it from opposite directions.
Predict specific behaviour from facet scores rather than from a domain score, and say why the domain score cannot do that job.
State the bandwidth-fidelity trade-off: broad predictors suit broad outcomes, narrow predictors suit narrow ones.
Describe why the facet level is less settled and less reliably measured than the domain level.
Explain how a domain score depends on the questionnaire's item sampling as well as on the person.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout using native radios, selects, ranges and buttons; each observation is a fieldset whose legend carries the behaviour, so options are never announced orphaned; charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables carrying the same numbers, and every bar prints its own value; verdict tone stated in words as well as by border colour; changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Trait structure: what a broad domain score averages away, and the bandwidth-fidelity trade-off
simulationNotes: All people and scores are fictional, on an arbitrary 0-100 scale with no norms, no standard error and no reference sample. A domain score is modelled as the weighted mean of two facet scores; behavioural tendency is a linear function of facet scores with no error, no situational input and no trait interaction. Facet pair names are taken from a published two-aspect account of the Big Five so that students learn vocabulary that exists, but no published item, norm or finding is reproduced.
